Some effects change the **pitch** of a sound while it plays: an octave below to fatten a bass, a
harmony above a voice, or a nudge to put a singer exactly in tune. All of them start from the same
trick.

## How to change pitch without changing speed

Play a tape faster and it gets higher, but it also gets shorter. A **pitch shifter** wants the pitch
without the speed. It reads the sound through a short delay whose time keeps changing: a delay that
keeps getting *shorter* plays the sound back faster (higher), one that keeps getting *longer* plays it
slower (lower). That's the [Doppler effect](sound-chorus.qmd) again. Of course a delay can't keep
shrinking forever, so every few hundredths of a second it jumps back and starts again, and a second
delay line, half a step behind, crossfades over the jump. Listen closely to big shifts and you can hear
a faint flutter from the jumps: that's the price.

## The octaver

<div class="sk" data-w="octaver"></div>

The **octaver** adds the same notes an octave (or two) below, or above. Bass players use the octave
down to sound like a synth bass; guitarists use the octave up to sound like a twelve-string.

**Octave up made by**: there's an old analog trick. Fold the bottom half of the wave up so it's all
positive (a **rectifier**), and the wave now repeats twice as often: an octave up. It's rough and
buzzy, and it only works cleanly on one note at a time: **Octave fuzz** is the Jimi Hendrix "Purple
Haze" solo sound. Switch between the two kinds and compare. Play the **Chords** through each: the
digital shifter copes; the analog trick turns chords to mush.

## The harmonizer

<div class="sk" data-w="harmonizer" data-source="voice"></div>

A **harmonizer** adds one or two more voices at set intervals, so one singer becomes a trio.

- **Fixed intervals**: always the same distance, say a major third and a fifth. Sing a scale and
  listen: some of the harmonies are out of the key, because the thirds in a major key are not all the
  same size.
- **In the key of C major**: the harmonizer works out which note you're singing and picks the third or
  fifth *in the key*, sometimes major, sometimes minor. This is how the "intelligent" harmonizers
  (Eventide, TC-Helicon, the ones built into vocal pedals) work. Try your **Microphone** and sing a
  C major scale slowly.

## Pitch correction (auto-tune)

<div class="sk" data-w="autotune"></div>

The source is an **out-of-tune singer**: every note lands 20 to 50 cents sharp or flat. The graph
shows the pitch as sung (grey) and after correction (pink), against the notes of the scale.

- **Key** and **Scale**: which notes are "right". Every sung note is pulled to the nearest one.
- **Retune speed**: how quickly. At around 100 ms the correction is gentle: the slides and the vibrato
  survive, and you mostly can't tell. This is what happens, invisibly, on most pop vocals today.
- At **1 ms** the pitch jumps instantly from note to note, with no slide at all. It sounds robotic,
  and that became a style of its own: Cher's "Believe" (1998), T-Pain, Kanye West's *808s &
  Heartbreak*, much of trap and Afrobeats.
- **Wrong key**: correct to the wrong scale and the singer is snapped confidently onto wrong notes.

Antares Auto-Tune came out in 1997, invented by an engineer who had used the same mathematics to look
for oil underground. Try your own voice, on *Hard* and *Natural*.
